results.result: Disease modifying therapies (DMTs) have revolutionized treatment of relapsing-remitting MS but are less effective for progressive MS and brain atrophy.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C12-C14 establish the clinical context for MS treatment based on established knowledge and cited literature. These are well-accepted facts in the MS field supported by appropriate citations (Reich et al., 2018; Faissner et al., 2019).

results.result: Leptomeningeal inflammation (LMI) is associated with cortical gray matter pathology in MS, which causes cognitive impairment and depression, but the mechanisms remain unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C15-C26, C82-C83 establish the relationship between LMI and gray matter pathology based on well-cited prior literature (Howell et al., 2011; Absinta et al., 2015; Wicken et al., 2018; Geurts and Barkhof, 2008; Bø et al., 2003a,b; Magliozzi et al., 2010; Mainero et al., 2015; van Horssen et al., 2007; Pikor et al., 2015). This provides appropriate background and identifies the knowledge gap the study addresses.

results.result: Prior studies have identified specific cytokines, chemokines, and signaling pathways associated with meningeal inflammation and gray matter pathology in MS and animal models.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C31 summarize prior mechanistic studies with appropriate citations (Magliozzi et al., 2018, 2019; Storch et al., 2006; Merkler et al., 2006; Brink et al., 2005). These establish the state of knowledge regarding potential mechanisms linking LMI to gray matter damage.

results.result: The SJL mouse EAE model exhibits meningeal inflammation with adjacent parenchymal pathology, providing a suitable model for studying LMI mechanisms with spatial resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 establish the rationale for using the SJL EAE model and cite prior characterization work (Magliozzi et al., 2004; Bhargava et al., 2021). The identification of the methodological gap (lack of spatially resolved data, C32) justifies the current approach.

results.result: SJL mice developed characteristic relapsing EAE with stable meningeal lesions detected by MRI at weeks 6, 8, and 10, with tissue collected at week 11 for spatial transcriptomics.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39, C107-C111 describe the experimental timeline and disease course, supported by data in Figures 1B-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B. The behavioral data, MRI imaging, and lesion quantification provide appropriate characterization of the model.

results.result: CFA alone does not produce lasting glial reactivity or LMI formation, validating the use of naïve controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42, C97 address a potential confound by demonstrating that CFA alone does not induce the pathology of interest. This is supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E) showing no difference in GFAP, IBA1, or CD68 between naïve and CFA-only animals.

results.result: Spatial transcriptomic data from all samples were of high quality with appropriate anatomic variability and no batch effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46, C112-C115 describe quality control metrics supported by extensive supplementary data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-J). The methods describe appropriate filtering, normalization (SCTransform), and validation that sample/slide effects do not confound the analysis.

results.result: Numerous genes associated with complement, immune infiltration, antigen presentation, and astrocyte activation were differentially expressed between EAE and naïve samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48, C116 describe differential expression analysis using DESeq2 on pseudobulked samples, shown in Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2K-L, and Supplementary file 1. The use of pseudobulking and DESeq2 is appropriate for spatial transcriptomics data.

results.result: Inflammatory pathways (TNF, JAK-STAT, NFκB) were upregulated in EAE with peak activity at meningeal inflammation sites, while Trail and PI3K pathways were downregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52, C118 describe pathway analysis using PROGENy, shown in Figure 2. The spatial distribution of pathway activities and statistical comparisons between groups are clearly presented. PROGENy is an established method for pathway activity estimation from transcriptomics data.

results.result: Unbiased clustering identified cluster 11 (C11) as EAE-specific, representing 1-5% of spots, overlapping with MRI-identified meningeal inflammation.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 describe the identification of meningeal inflammation regions through unbiased clustering, supported by UMAP plots (Figure 3A-D) and spatial correlation with MRI (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D). The inference that C11 represents meningeal inflammation (C58) is reasonable given the spatial overlap with MRI enhancement.

results.result: Cluster 11 showed enrichment of inflammation-related genes (Cd74, C3, Gfap) and gene sets related to antigen processing/presentation, complement activation, lymphocyte activation, and cytokine signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C66 characterize the transcriptional signature of meningeal inflammation, supported by differential expression analysis (Figure 3F-G, Supplementary file 2) and gene set enrichment analysis (Figure 3H, Supplementary file 3). The interpretation regarding Gfap (C62) acknowledges the spatial resolution limitation. The comparison to human data (C64) is appropriately cited.

results.result: EAE-specific subclusters (1_3, 1_4, 2_6) were identified in thalamus and hypothalamus regions, with subcluster 2_6 significantly closer to meningeal inflammation.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 describe subclustering analysis identifying regions of inflamed parenchyma adjacent to LMI, supported by UMAP plots (Figure 4A-B), spatial plots (Figure 4C), and distance analysis (Figure 4D). The statistical comparison of proximity to C11 is appropriate.

results.result: EAE-specific subclusters showed enrichment of pathways related to inflammation, antigen processing/presentation, humoral immunity, neuron death, and cellular stress, with 31 pathways conserved between meningeal inflammation and adjacent parenchyma.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74, C117 characterize the transcriptional programs in inflamed parenchyma using gene set enrichment analysis (Figure 4E-I, Supplementary files 4-6). The identification of conserved pathways (C73-C74) provides insight into which inflammatory signals penetrate from meninges into parenchyma. The spatial variability in apoptotic pathways (C72) is an interesting observation.

results.result: Trajectory analysis revealed variable penetration of inflammatory gene sets from meninges into parenchyma, with antigen processing/presentation, cell killing, IL-6, and IFNγ response showing gradual decline, while C3 declined more rapidly than B2m.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78, C119 describe trajectory modeling using SPATA2 to quantify how inflammatory signals decay with distance from LMI (Figure 5A-F). The comparison of residual AUC for different decay patterns provides quantitative assessment of penetration depth. This is a novel analytical approach for spatial transcriptomics data.

results.result: RNAscope validation in an independent cohort confirmed differential penetration patterns, with C3 showing steeper exponential decline (b=-1.13) than B2m (b=-0.59) with distance from LMI.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81, C120 describe orthogonal validation using RNAscope in a separate cohort (Figure 5G-J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 7). The exponential regression analysis quantifies decay rates and confirms the spatial transcriptomics findings. This validation strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: The spatial resolution of ~55 μm per spot means multiple cells are captured in each spot, limiting cellular resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 acknowledge a key technical limitation of the 10x Visium platform. This is an accurate description of the technology and appropriately discussed as a limitation. The authors correctly note that single-cell deconvolution would improve interpretation.

results.result: Prior work supports roles for B cells and IFNγ signaling in MS neurodegeneration through multiple mechanisms including cytokine production, antibody-mediated toxicity, and upregulation of antigen presentation on glia.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C96 discuss the biological interpretation of findings in the context of prior literature, with appropriate citations (Lisak et al., 2017; Benjamins et al., 2019; Bhargava et al., 2022; Arellano et al., 2015; Kirby et al., 2019; Schirmer et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2018; Jäkel et al., 2019; Langseth et al., 2023; Kukanja et al., 2024; Lerma-Martin et al., 2022). This contextualizes the current findings within the broader field.

results.result: LMI in SJL EAE predominantly affects deep gray matter (thalamus/hypothalamus) rather than cortex, though similar surface-in gradients of pathology occur in human MS thalamus.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 acknowledge important differences between the mouse model and human disease, supported by the experimental observations and citations to human studies (Azevedo et al., 2018; Magliozzi et al., 2022; Bhargava et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2023). This is an appropriate discussion of model limitations and translatability.

results.result: This is the first spatial transcriptomic characterization of a mouse LMI model, contributing a publicly available dataset, with future applications possible using FFPE tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C106 discuss novelty and future directions. While the claim of being 'first' (C104) cannot be fully verified without comprehensive literature review, the approach appears novel. The statement about data availability (C105) is verifiable. The discussion of FFPE applications (C106) is appropriately cited but represents future potential rather than current results.

results.result: Multiple comparison correction was performed using the Benjamini-Hochberg method.
results.evaluation: Claim C121 describes the statistical correction method with appropriate citation (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). This is a standard and appropriate method for controlling false discovery rate in multiple testing scenarios common in transcriptomics studies.

results.result: The authors used MRI-guided spatial transcriptomics in the SJL mouse EAE model to characterize meningeal inflammation and adjacent brain parenchyma. The model exhibited relapsing neurologic impairment, contrast-enhancing meningeal lesions in specific anatomical locations, and high-quality spatial transcriptomic data with appropriate quality control metrics.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers acknowledge and accept the experimental approach and model characterization. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'use a spatial transcriptomics approach using Visium Gene Expression technology' and notes 'MRI imaging using a high field strength (11.7T) scanner was used to identify areas of meningeal infiltration.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'they use novel technology called spatial transcriptomics so that the spatial relationships between the two regions remain intact.' No concerns are raised about the model or data quality.

results.result: Differential gene expression analysis revealed upregulation of genes associated with complement cascade, immune infiltration, antigen presentation, and astrocyte activation in EAE samples. Pathway analysis showed upregulation of TNF, JAK-STAT, and NFκB signaling with peak activity around sites of meningeal inflammation, while Trail and PI3K pathways were downregulated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly confirm these findings. Reviewer 1 states 'They report, as might be expected, the upregulation of genes associated with the complement cascade, immune cell infiltration, antigen presentation, and astrocyte activation. Pathway analysis revealed the presence of TNF, JAK-STAT and NFkB signaling, amongst others, close to sites of meningeal inflammation.' The editor notes the study provides 'solid evidence for a gradient of immune genes and inflammatory markers from the meninges toward the adjacent brain parenchyma.'

results.result: UMAP clustering identified cluster 11 (C11) as EAE-specific, representing areas of meningeal inflammation that overlap with MRI enhancement. C11 showed upregulation of 132 genes including inflammation-related genes (Cd74, C3, Gfap), immunoglobulin genes, and enrichment of gene sets related to antigen processing/presentation, complement activation, lymphocyte activation, and cytokine production.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 confirms 'UMAP clustering illuminated a major distinct cluster of upregulated genes in the meninges' and notes 'The meningeal cluster contained genes associated with immune cell functions and interactions, cytokine production, and action.' Reviewer 2 states 'The study identifies canonical inflammatory genes and gene sets such as complement and B cells enriched in the parenchyma in close proximity to the leptomeninges.' No concerns are raised about the clustering or gene identification.

results.result: Subclustering analysis identified EAE-specific subclusters (1_3, 1_4, 2_6) in thalamus and hypothalamus regions adjacent to meningeal inflammation. These subclusters showed enrichment of pathways related to inflammation, antigen processing/presentation, humoral immunity, neuron death, and cellular stress, with 31 pathways conserved between meningeal inflammation and adjacent parenchyma.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly confirms these findings: 'The parenchymal clusters included genes and pathways related to glial activation, but also adaptive/B-cell mediated immunity and antigen presentation.' Reviewer 2 notes the study 'identifies canonical inflammatory genes and gene sets such as complement and B cells enriched in the parenchyma in close proximity to the leptomeninges.' The subclustering approach and findings are accepted without critique.

results.result: Trajectory analysis demonstrated variable penetration of immune signatures from meningeal inflammation into adjacent brain tissue, with different genes showing distinct spatial gradients. C3 expression declined rapidly (logarithmic pattern) while B2m showed a more gradual decline (gradient pattern). RNAscope validation confirmed these differential spatial patterns with exponential decay of transcript-positive cells with distance from meningeal inflammation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly confirms 'a trajectory analysis based on distance from the meningeal gene cluster successfully demonstrated descending and ascending gradients of gene expression, in particular a decline in pathway enrichment for immune processes with distance from the meninges.' The editor emphasizes the study provides 'solid evidence for a gradient of immune genes and inflammatory markers from the meninges toward the adjacent brain parenchyma.' The validation by RNAscope is accepted without critique.

results.result: Inflammatory signaling pathways are broadly increased at sites of meningeal inflammation, but only a subset of these pathways (notably complement signaling and antigen processing/presentation) are active in the adjacent brain parenchyma.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the findings, Reviewer 1 raises a technical concern about spatial resolution: 'the spatial resolution is insufficient to indicate whether this is in the meninges, grey matter, or both' and notes 'This again suggests a technical inability to resolve fully between the compartments as immune cells do not penetrate the pial surface in this model or in MS.' This limitation creates uncertainty about whether the observed signals truly represent parenchymal activity versus meningeal contamination.

results.result: The spatial transcriptomics method has a spatial resolution of approximately 55 μm per spot, meaning multiple cells are likely captured in each spot. This technical limitation affects interpretation of whether signals originate from meninges or adjacent parenchyma.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly acknowledges this limitation, stating 'the spatial resolution is insufficient to indicate whether this is in the meninges, grey matter, or both' and 'This again suggests a technical inability to resolve fully between the compartments.' The authors themselves acknowledge this limitation in the manuscript. This is treated as an accepted technical constraint of the methodology rather than a flaw in execution.

results.result: In the SJL EAE model, leptomeningeal inflammation predominantly occurred in subarachnoid cisterns affecting deep gray matter (thalamus and hypothalamus) rather than cortical regions. Despite this anatomical difference from human MS, the model shows demyelination, glial activation, and neuronal loss in parenchyma adjacent to meningeal inflammation, and human MS also exhibits similar 'surface-in' gradients of neuronal injury in deep gray nuclei.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the model characteristics without raising concerns about its validity. Reviewer 1 notes the study uses 'the PLP-induced EAE model of MS in the SJL mouse' and accepts the findings. Reviewer 2 states 'This study aims to understand the local immune hallmarks in regions of the brain parenchyma that are adjacent to the leptomeninges in a mouse model of MS.' The anatomical differences are presented as acknowledged limitations rather than fundamental flaws.

results.result: Background claims establishing that meningeal inflammation is a recognized risk factor for gray matter pathology in MS, that disease-modifying therapies are less effective for progressive MS, and that the mechanisms linking meningeal inflammation to gray matter pathology remain unclear.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these background statements without challenge. Reviewer 1 states 'Accumulating data suggests that the presence of immune cell infiltrates in the meninges of the multiple sclerosis brain contributes to the tissue damage in the underlying cortical grey matter' and notes 'little is known about the identity and direct and indirect effects of these mediators at a molecular level.' These are treated as established context for the study.

results.result: This work is the first to characterize a mouse model of leptomeningeal inflammation and gray matter injury using spatial transcriptomics and contributes a publicly available dataset for future research.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the novelty and value of the approach. The editor states this is 'an important study' that 'advances our understanding of the mechanisms of brain damage in this autoimmune disease.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The results will become a useful resource to others working in the field and can be followed by time series experiments where the same technology can be applied to the different stages of the disease.' The novelty claim is implicitly accepted.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on claims C98-C101 regarding model limitations and differences between mouse EAE and human MS. Both evaluations accept these as acknowledged limitations rather than fundamental flaws, with appropriate discussion of translatability concerns.

Strong overlap on background claims C1-C5, C12-C26 establishing MS clinical context and LMI-gray matter pathology relationship. Both evaluations support these as well-established background with appropriate citations, treating them as accepted context for the study.

Partial overlap on clinical background claims C1-C2, C12-C14. Both evaluations accept these as established MS facts. OpenEval groups these with additional background claims while peer review combines them with broader literature context.

Strong agreement on technical limitation claims C84-C85 regarding Visium spatial resolution. Both evaluations acknowledge this as an inherent platform constraint appropriately discussed by authors, not an execution flaw. Peer review also includes C62 (Gfap interpretation) as related to this limitation.

Minimal overlap on C62 regarding Gfap interpretation. OpenEval includes this in broader meningeal characterization (R11) as appropriately acknowledging resolution limits, while peer review groups it with technical limitations (R7).

Strong agreement on pathway analysis claims C49-C52 showing TNF, JAK-STAT, NFkB signaling near meningeal inflammation. Both evaluations support these findings as expected and well-demonstrated. Peer review explicitly confirms upregulation of complement, immune infiltration, and pathway findings.

Partial overlap on differential expression analysis claims C47-C48. Both evaluations support the DESeq2 pseudobulking approach and findings. OpenEval focuses on methodological appropriateness while peer review emphasizes biological interpretation of results.

Strong agreement on meningeal inflammation identification claims C53-C58 through unbiased clustering and MRI correlation. Both evaluations support the clustering approach and spatial inference that C11 represents meningeal inflammation without raising concerns.

Strong agreement on meningeal transcriptional characterization claims C59-C66. Both evaluations confirm identification of immune-related genes, cytokine production, and inflammatory signatures in meningeal cluster. Peer review explicitly validates these findings without critique.

Strong agreement on subclustering claims C67-C69 identifying inflamed parenchyma adjacent to LMI. Both evaluations support the approach and spatial proximity findings. Peer review confirms parenchymal clusters show glial activation and adaptive immunity.

Strong agreement on parenchymal transcriptional programs claims C70-C74. Both evaluations support gene set enrichment findings showing complement, B-cell immunity, and antigen presentation in parenchyma near meninges. Peer review explicitly confirms these canonical inflammatory signatures.

Strong agreement on trajectory analysis claims C75-C78 demonstrating gradient decay of inflammatory signals with distance from LMI. Both evaluations support this novel analytical approach. Peer review explicitly confirms descending gradients of immune pathway enrichment.

Strong agreement on RNAscope validation claims C79-C81. Both evaluations accept the orthogonal validation confirming spatial transcriptomics findings through exponential regression analysis in separate cohort. Editor emphasizes solid evidence for gradient.

Agreement on SJL EAE model rationale claims C32-C35. Both evaluations support the model choice and characterization. Peer review confirms acceptance of experimental approach without concerns about model validity.

Agreement on experimental timeline and disease course claims C36-C39, C107-C111. Both evaluations support the model characterization with behavioral data, MRI, and lesion quantification. Peer review explicitly accepts the high-field MRI approach.

Agreement on CFA control claims C40-C42, C97. Both evaluations support the demonstration that CFA alone does not induce pathology. Peer review accepts this control without raising concerns about experimental design.

Agreement on quality control claims C43-C46, C112-C115. Both evaluations support the QC metrics, filtering, and normalization approaches. Peer review confirms acceptance of data quality and spatial transcriptomics methodology.

Agreement on novelty and data availability claims C104-C105. Both evaluations acknowledge the novel approach and value to the field. Peer review emphasizes this as important study advancing understanding and providing useful resource, implicitly accepting novelty claims.

OpenEval supports claims C27-C31 summarizing prior mechanistic studies linking LMI to gray matter damage with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these background mechanism claims.

OpenEval supports claims C86-C96 discussing biological interpretation in context of oligodendrocyte biology, remyelination, and prior literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these discussion points.
OpenEval supports claim C121 regarding Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction method. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this statistical methodology detail.

Peer review raises uncertainty about claims C7-C10 regarding spatial resolution limitations in distinguishing meningeal versus parenchymal signals, noting immune cells do not penetrate pial surface. No corresponding OpenEval result specifically addresses these claims about potential compartment contamination.
